frozen_original.title: Trump Threatens to Deploy National Guard to 2026 Midterm Polling Places
frozen_original.synopsis: In a January 7, 2026 New York Times interview, Trump expressed regret that he had not directed the National Guard to seize voting machines after the 2020 election, signaling his intent to use military force around the 2026 midterms. Trump had already deployed the National Guard to at least four Democratic-led cities against the will of their governors in 2025, with courts issuing multiple injunctions. A February 2026 PBS News report revealed a 17-page draft executive order circulating among Trump allies that would declare a national emergency to take federal control over midterm elections, require hand-counting of ballots, and force voters to re-register with proof of citizenship. Trump publicly threatened on Truth Social: 'There will be Voter I.D. for the Midterm Elections, whether approved by Congress or not!' Legal experts said any troop deployment to polls would violate multiple federal statutes.

primary.title: Trump Allies Circulate Draft Election Emergency Order; Trump Says He Is Not Considering It
primary.description_short: PBS reported a 17-page draft order among Trump allies proposed emergency powers over the 2026 midterms; Trump said he was not considering declaring an emergency.
primary.description_medium: PBS News reported on February 27, 2026, that a 17-page draft executive order circulating among Trump allies proposed declaring a national emergency to expand federal control over parts of the 2026 midterm elections. The draft included hand-counting and voter-identification provisions. PBS reported that Trump said he was not considering declaring an emergency around the midterms. The source describes a proposal, not an order Trump enacted.
primary.description_long: On February 27, 2026, PBS News reported that a 17-page draft executive order was circulating among Trump allies. PBS said it reviewed the working document. The draft proposed declaring a national emergency and using it to assert federal control over parts of the 2026 midterm election process. Provisions described by PBS included hand-counted ballots, voter identification, and voter re-registration with proof of citizenship. The article presented these as elements of a proposal, not as changes that had taken effect. PBS reported that Trump said he was not considering declaring a national emergency around the midterms; in his reported response to a question about the draft, he said, “Who told you that?” Peter Ticktin, a Trump ally, confirmed to PBS that the draft had circulated among some supporters. The record therefore concerns circulation of a draft by allies and public reporting about Trump’s response. It does not establish that Trump ordered the draft, adopted it, deployed National Guard troops at polling places, or changed election administration under it. This entry makes no claim that the draft was enacted or implemented.

frozen_original.title: US and Israeli Airstrikes on Iranian Nuclear Facilities
frozen_original.synopsis: In June 2025, the United States and Israel conducted coordinated airstrikes targeting Iran's nuclear infrastructure in the most significant military operation against Iran in history. The strikes targeted enrichment facilities, research reactors, and weapons development sites across multiple locations. The operation involved US B-2 stealth bombers, Israeli F-35 aircraft, and cruise missiles launched from naval vessels. Trump announced the strikes in a late-night social media post before official notification to congressional leadership, further violating War Powers Act requirements. The operation triggered immediate Iranian retaliation and pushed the Middle East to the brink of a regional war involving multiple nation-states.

primary.split_rationale: The frozen entry joined Israel’s campaign beginning June 13 to the later U.S. strikes across June 21–22. The sources document separate actors, dates, and operations, so the record is split into one child for each campaign. The claimed jointly executed operation beginning June 13 and the War Powers allegation are omitted because the accessed sources do not establish them.

children.title: Israel Begins Strikes on Iran’s Nuclear and Military Sites
children.description_short: Israel began strikes against Iranian nuclear and military sites on June 13, 2025, including reported damage to underground structures at Natanz.
children.description_medium: On June 13, 2025, Israel began a strike campaign against Iranian nuclear facilities and military sites. Al Jazeera reported an initial Friday-morning wave and a separate later attack on Tabriz; it also attributed reported damage at Natanz to Israel’s military and described damage to residential buildings. This entry covers Israel’s opening action. U.S. forces struck Iranian nuclear sites on June 21–22 in a separate operation, recorded in another child.
children.description_long: Israel began strikes on Iran on June 13, 2025, targeting nuclear facilities and military sites, according to Al Jazeera’s contemporaneous report. The report described an initial wave early Friday and a later, separate strike on Tabriz. It said Israel’s military claimed that its attacks damaged underground structures at the Natanz uranium-enrichment site and struck missile infrastructure; the Iranian Atomic Energy Organization said radioactive contamination from the Natanz strike remained within the site. The article also described damage to residential buildings, while casualty figures attributed to Iranian state media were presented as unofficial estimates and are not repeated here. The supplied record incorrectly combined this Israeli campaign with a later U.S. operation. U.S. forces struck Iranian nuclear sites on June 21 in Washington and June 22 in Tehran, a separate action recorded in another child. This entry does not describe the two operations as coordinated or jointly executed, and it omits claims about congressional notification and War Powers violations that the accessed source does not establish.

children.title: United States Strikes Iranian Nuclear Sites in Operation Midnight Hammer
children.description_short: U.S. forces struck Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan in an operation spanning June 21 in Washington and June 22 in Tehran, according to AP reporting published by PBS.
children.description_medium: U.S. forces struck Iranian nuclear facilities in Operation Midnight Hammer. The Associated Press, published by PBS NewsHour on June 22, reported that B-2 bombers attacked Fordow and Natanz while submarine-launched Tomahawk missiles hit targets including Isfahan. The first bomber’s strike occurred at 6:40 p.m. in Washington and 2:10 a.m. in Tehran, so the operation crossed a local-date boundary. U.S. officials’ damage claims and Iran’s denial are kept distinct.
children.description_long: On June 21–22, 2025, U.S. forces launched Operation Midnight Hammer against Iranian nuclear facilities. An Associated Press report published by PBS NewsHour described B-2 stealth bombers dropping bunker-buster bombs on the underground Fordow and Natanz enrichment sites and submarine-launched Tomahawk missiles striking targets including Isfahan. The report placed the first bomber’s strike at 6:40 p.m. in Washington and 2:10 a.m. in Tehran, explaining why some accounts date the operation June 21 and others June 22. U.S. officials described the attack as devastating Iran’s nuclear program, but the same report said assessments were ongoing and Iran denied significant damage. The entry therefore records the strikes and weapons reported, not a settled conclusion about the program’s condition. The U.S. operation followed nine days of Israeli attacks, according to AP, but it was a distinct action. The original card’s claim that both countries conducted one coordinated operation beginning June 13 is not supported by these sources. Claims about congressional notification and a War Powers Act violation are also omitted because the accessed report does not establish them.

It said Israel’s military claimed that its attacks damaged underground structures at the Natanz uranium-enrichment site and struck missile infrastructure; the Iranian Atomic Energy Organization said radioactive contamination from the Natanz strike remained within the site. The article also described damage to residential buildings, while casualty figures attributed to Iranian state media were presented as unofficial estimates and are not repeated here. The supplied record incorrectly combined this Israeli campaign with a later U.S. operation. U.S. forces struck Iranian nuclear sites on June 21 in Washington and June 22 in Tehran, a separate action recorded in another child. This entry does not describe the two operations as coordinated or jointly executed, and it omits claims about congressional notification and War Powers violations that the accessed source does not establish.

children.title: United States Strikes Iranian Nuclear Sites in Operation Midnight Hammer
children.description_short: U.S. forces struck Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan in an operation spanning June 21 in Washington and June 22 in Tehran, according to AP reporting published by PBS.
children.description_medium: U.S. forces struck Iranian nuclear facilities in Operation Midnight Hammer. The Associated Press, published by PBS NewsHour on June 22, reported that B-2 bombers attacked Fordow and Natanz while submarine-launched Tomahawk missiles hit targets including Isfahan. The first bomber’s strike occurred at 6:40 p.m. in Washington and 2:10 a.m. in Tehran, so the operation crossed a local-date boundary. U.S. officials’ damage claims and Iran’s denial are kept distinct.
children.description_long: On June 21–22, 2025, U.S. forces launched Operation Midnight Hammer against Iranian nuclear facilities. An Associated Press report published by PBS NewsHour described B-2 stealth bombers dropping bunker-buster bombs on the underground Fordow and Natanz enrichment sites and submarine-launched Tomahawk missiles striking targets including Isfahan. The report placed the first bomber’s strike at 6:40 p.m. in Washington and 2:10 a.m. in Tehran, explaining why some accounts date the operation June 21 and others June 22. U.S. officials described the attack as devastating Iran’s nuclear program, but the same report said assessments were ongoing and Iran denied significant damage. The entry therefore records the strikes and weapons reported, not a settled conclusion about the program’s condition. The U.S. operation followed nine days of Israeli attacks, according to AP, but it was a distinct action. The original card’s claim that both countries conducted one coordinated operation beginning June 13 is not supported by these sources. Claims about congressional notification and a War Powers Act violation are also omitted because the accessed report does not establish them.

frozen_original.title: Trump Fires All 93 US Attorneys on Day One — Installs Loyalists
frozen_original.synopsis: On January 20, 2025, the Trump administration fired all 93 sitting U.S. Attorneys across the country — the chief federal prosecutors in every judicial district — and replaced them with Trump loyalists and former personal attorneys, some of whom lacked federal prosecution experience and were selected primarily for their political allegiance. While transitions between administrations typically involve some U.S. Attorney replacements, the simultaneous firing of all 93 with no transition period was unprecedented in modern history. Career federal prosecutors in multiple districts reported being given no notice and losing access to case systems within hours. Ongoing public corruption cases, organized crime prosecutions, and civil rights cases were left in limbo. The mass replacement ensured that federal prosecution decisions in every district would henceforth be filtered through political loyalty to the President rather than legal merit — fundamentally transforming the federal prosecutorial system.

primary.title: White House Terminates Some U.S. Attorneys in February 2025
primary.description_short: NBC reported the White House terminated as many as a dozen U.S. attorneys on February 12, 2025; the reported total was not established.
primary.description_medium: On February 12, 2025, the White House terminated some U.S. attorneys during a wider change in federal prosecutorial leadership. NBC News reported terminations of as many as a dozen and said the precise total was not immediately available. Its account described immediate White House dismissals as a departure from the usual practice of Justice Department resignation requests.
primary.description_long: On the evening of February 12, 2025, the White House terminated some U.S. attorneys during a transition in federal prosecutorial leadership. NBC News reported that the removals may have affected as many as a dozen offices and said its review found twelve names changed from a list published two days earlier. The Justice Department had not provided a total for how many of the nation’s 93 U.S. attorneys were affected. The article also noted that remaining Biden-nominated, Senate-confirmed attorneys were expected to leave, while immediate White House terminations departed from the usual practice of Justice Department resignation requests. This narrows the stored claim that all 93 attorneys were fired on January 20: the accessed reporting places terminations three weeks later and describes a limited number, not a complete one-day purge. It does not establish that all displaced attorneys were replaced by loyalists, that offices’ pending cases were left in limbo, or that prosecutors’ work was thereafter filtered through political loyalty. NBC reported that officials had not provided a final count. The account describes a personnel action and its reported departure from customary transitions, without asserting a legal finding about its propriety.
primary.date_basis: The NBC article is dated February 13, 2025 and identifies the terminations as occurring Wednesday evening.
